newsitem.title: USA: CVS, Revco confirm merger talks. [CORRECTED 23:35 GMT]
newsitem.headline: CVS, Revco confirm merger talks. [CORRECTED 23:35 GMT]

text.p: Revco D.S. Inc., the second largest U.S. drugstore chain, is in talks to be acquired by CVS Corp., which ranks fifth, the companies said Monday.

The companies did not elaborate on any potential terms of merger and warned a final deal might not be struck. Revco and CVS said neither would comment further until a deal is reached or the talks are terminated.

Nationally, Revco is second only to Rite Aid Corp. in the number of stores, and has 2,600 drugstores in 17 states, mainly in the eastern United States, and home health care stores. The Twinsburg, Ohio-based company rang up sales of about $5.08 billion in the year ended June 1.
CVS, based in Woonsocket, R.I., has 1,408 drug stores in 15 Northeastern and Middle Atlantic states and the District of Columbia. It had sales of about $9.7 billion in 1995.
The company, formerly Melville Corp., spun off a footwear business, discontinued some other businesses and in October changed its name to CVS, retaining the drug stores.

The CVS-Revco combination is almost certain to draw heavy scrutiny from the Federal Trade Commission and other federal regulatory agencies. But overall, analysts said the deal was unlikely to face major regulatory hurdles since there is little geographic overlap.
CVS also will need to woo Revco Vice Chairman Sam Zell, the investor whose Zell/Chilmark Fund LP owns about 20 percent of Revco stock.
Analysts said a merger would make sense because it would put the combined company on a more even footing with other giant drug chains in a consolidating industry.
If a deal occurs, it could bring up to $45 a share for Revco shareholders including Zell, they said.
Revco shares spiked up early Monday but closed 37.5 cents lower at $38.875 on the New York Stock Exchange. CVS slid 12.5 cents to $42.875, also on the NYSE.
"It could be worth $44 to $45" for Revco shareholders, said J.P. Morgan Securities analyst Mark Husson.

If successful, the acquisition by CVS would mark a sharp reversal of roles for Revco, which is still settling in with its acquisition of Big B Inc (corrects by removing incorrect reference to Revco trying to buy out Rite Aid).
Revco last month bought Alabama-based Big B Inc. in a deal valued at $380 million. With its nearly 400 stores, Big B brought Revco to 2,600 stores in the Midwest and Southeast.
Drug store chains are merging to fight drug pricing pressures in the era of managed care and health maintenance organisations.

Antitrust regulators' concerns about overlapping markets derailed a Rite Aid Corp. friendly $1.8 billion bid for Revco last year. Rite Aid later acquired Thrifty Payless in a deal valued at $1.4 billion, giving Rite Aid more than 3,500 stores with annual revenues of more than $10 billion.

Another $10 billion-plus behemoth, Walgreen Co., has largely sat out consolidation, focusing instead on opening new stores for growth. The third giant is J.C. Penney Co.'s Thrift Drug Inc. which is buying Eckerd Corp.
With the failed Rite Aid deal, Revco made it known it could be for sale, and with all the mergers in the industry, the list of available targets has dwindled, analysts said.
"Companies are not just buying earnings per share. They are buying leverage against the big third-party plan managers," J.P. Morgan's Husson said.

Merrill Lynch's Gary Vineberg, who follows the drug store industry but does not follow CVS or Revco, said smaller companies fear if they don't participate in the "merger and acquisition frenzy," they may become too small to compete effectively.
